title: Charlotte Capital Connection 2026
text:
Analysis code
Download R script
The script requires tidyverse, knitr, scales, and uuid. Place guest_registration.csv, faculty_staff_registration.csv, and employer_registration_counts.csv in a data folder beneath your R working directory. The registration datasets are not included here.


View R code

# Charlotte Capital Connection 2026 — Registration & Engagement Report
# Joseph Falcone
# Place the three cleaned registration CSVs in a data/ folder
# beneath your R working directory. Datasets are not included.

library(tidyverse)

guests <- read_csv('data/guest_registration.csv')
faculty <- read_csv('data/faculty_staff_registration.csv')
employer <- read_csv('data/employer_registration_counts.csv')

# Events
event_colors <- c(
    'Both' = '#FF8200',
    'Networking Reception' = '#489FDF',
    'Fireside Chat' = '#236A9A'
)

# UT Affiliation
affiliation_colors <- c(
    'alumni' = '#FF8200',
    'alumni_employer_partner' = '#E65C00',
    'current_student' = '#E8A86D',
    'employer_partner' = '#4D4D4D',
    'alumni_current_student' = '#994500'
)

# Graduation Decade
decade_colors <- c(
    '1980s' = '#663300',
    '1990s' = '#994500',
    '2000s' = '#C96500',
    '2010s' = '#FF8200',
    '2020s' = '#FFB366'
)

# Academic Programs
program_colors <- c(
    '#FF8200',  # Tennessee Orange
    '#489FDF',  # Summitt Blue
    '#4D4D4D',  # Smokey Gray
    '#E65C00',  # Vibrant Orange
    '#236A9A',  # Dark Blue
    '#A7A9AC',  # Light Gray
    '#FFB366',  # Light Orange
    '#6C5B7B',  # Muted Purple
    '#00857D',  # Teal
    '#B35C8D',  # Muted Magenta
    '#6B8E23',  # Olive Green
    '#D4A017',  # Golden Yellow
    '#395C6B',  # Slate Blue
    '#9B6A45'   # Warm Brown
)

# Haslam Undergraduate
undergrad_colors <- c(
    'TRUE' = '#FF8200',
    'FALSE' = '#4D4D4D'
)

# Alumni Status
alumni_colors <- c(
    'Alumni' = '#FF8200',
    'Non-Alumni' = '#4D4D4D'
)

# Event Registration Type
selection_colors <- c(
    'Both Events' = '#FF8200',
    'One Event' = '#4D4D4D'
)

# bar chart
guests |>
    ggplot(aes(
        x = fct_infreq(ut_affiliation),
        fill = fct_infreq(ut_affiliation)
    )) +
    geom_bar() +
    geom_text(
        stat = 'count',
        aes(label = after_stat(count)),
        vjust = -0.3
    ) + 
    scale_fill_manual(
        values = affiliation_colors
    ) +
    scale_y_continuous(
        expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.1))
    ) +
    labs(
        title = 'Registrant Count by Affiliation',
        x = 'UT Affiliation',
        y = 'Count'
    ) +
    theme_minimal()

guests |>
    filter(!is.na(grad_year)) |>
    mutate(decade = paste0(floor(grad_year / 10) * 10, 's')) |>
    count(decade) |>
    mutate(proportion = n / sum(n)) |>
    ggplot(aes(x = decade, y = proportion, fill = decade)) +
    geom_col() +
    geom_text(
        aes(label = scales::percent(proportion, accuracy = 0.1)),
        vjust = -0.3
    ) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = decade_colors) +
    scale_y_continuous(
        labels = scales::label_percent(),
        expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.1))
    ) +
    labs(
        title = 'Registrant Proportion by Graduation Decade',
        x = 'Graduation Decade',
        y = 'Proportion'
    ) +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(legend.position = 'none')

guests |>
    filter(!is.na(grad_year)) |>
    mutate(decade = paste0(floor(as.numeric(grad_year) / 10) * 10, 's')) |>
    count(decade) |>
    knitr::kable(
        col.names = c('Graduation Decade', 'Registrants'),
        caption = 'Registrants by Graduation Decade'
    )

# bar chart
guests |>
    filter(!is.na(programs)) |>
    ggplot(aes(
        x = fct_infreq(programs),
        fill = fct_infreq(programs)
    )) +
    geom_bar() +
    geom_text(
        stat = 'count',
        aes(label = after_stat(count)),
        hjust = -0.3
    ) +
    scale_fill_manual(
        values = program_colors
    ) +
    scale_y_continuous(
        expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))
    ) +
    coord_flip() +
    labs(
        title = 'Registrant Count by Program',
        x = 'Program',
        y = 'Count'
    ) +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(legend.position = 'none')

guests |>
    filter(!is.na(haslam_undergrad)) |>
    ggplot(aes(
        x = '',
        fill = as.factor(haslam_undergrad)
    )) +
    geom_bar(width = 1) +
    geom_text(
        stat = 'count',
        aes(
            label = scales::percent(after_stat(count / sum(count)), accuracy = 0.1)
        ),
        position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5),
        color = 'white'
    ) +
    coord_polar(theta = 'y') +
    scale_fill_manual(
        values = undergrad_colors
    ) +
    labs(
        title = 'Haslam Undergraduate Affiliation',
        fill = 'Haslam Undergraduate'
    ) +
    theme_void()

guests |>
    filter(!is.na(events)) |>
    mutate(
        fireside_chat = events %in% c('Fireside Chat', 'Both'),
        networking_reception = events %in% c('Networking Reception', 'Both')
    ) |>
    pivot_longer(
        cols = c(fireside_chat, networking_reception),
        names_to = 'event',
        values_to = 'registered'
    ) |>
    filter(registered) |>
    mutate(
        selection = if_else(events == 'Both', 'Both Events', 'One Event')
    ) |>
    count(event, selection) |>
    ggplot(aes(x = event, y = n, fill = selection)) +
    geom_col() +
    geom_text(
        aes(label = n),
        position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5),
        color = 'white'
    ) +
    geom_text(
        aes(
            x = event,
            y = n,
            group = event,
            label = after_stat(y)
        ),
        stat = 'summary',
        fun = sum,
        inherit.aes = FALSE,
        vjust = -0.5
    ) +
    scale_fill_manual(
        values = selection_colors
    ) +
    scale_y_continuous(
        expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))
    ) +
    labs(
        title = 'Event Registrations by Selection Type',
        x = 'Event',
        y = 'Registrations',
        fill = 'Registration Type',
        caption = 'Note: Registrants selecting both events are counted in each event total.'
    ) +
    theme_minimal()

guests |>
    filter(!is.na(events), !is.na(grad_year)) |>
    mutate(
        decade = paste0(floor(as.numeric(grad_year) / 10) * 10, 's')
    ) |>
    ggplot(aes(
        x = decade,
        fill = events
    )) +
    geom_bar() +
    geom_text(
        stat = 'count',
        aes(label = after_stat(count)),
        position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5),
        color = 'white'
    ) +
    scale_fill_manual(
        values = event_colors
    ) +
    scale_y_continuous(
        expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.1))
    ) +
    labs(
        title = 'Event Selection by Graduation Decade',
        x = 'Graduation Decade',
        y = 'Registrants',
        fill = 'Event Selection'
    ) +
    theme_minimal()

guests |>
    filter(!is.na(employer), employer != '') |>
    add_count(employer, name = 'total') |>
    filter(total > 1) |>
    mutate(
        alumni_status = if_else(
            ut_affiliation %in% c(
                'alumni',
                'alumni_current_student',
                'alumni_employer_partner'
            ),
            'Alumni',
            'Non-Alumni'
        )
    ) |>
    count(employer, alumni_status, total) |>
    ggplot(aes(
        x = fct_reorder(employer, total),
        y = n,
        fill = alumni_status
    )) +
    geom_col() +
    geom_text(
        aes(label = n),
        position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5),
        color = 'white'
    ) +
    scale_fill_manual(
        values = alumni_colors
    ) +
    coord_flip() +
    labs(
        title = 'Employer Representation by Alumni Status',
        x = 'Employer',
        y = 'Registrants',
        fill = 'Alumni Status'
    ) +
    theme_minimal()

employer |>
    mutate(total = both + fireside_chat_only + networking_only) |>
    filter(total > 1) |>
    pivot_longer(
        cols = c(both, fireside_chat_only, networking_only),
        names_to = 'event',
        values_to = 'n'
    ) |>
    ggplot(aes(
        x = fct_reorder(employer, total),
        y = n,
        fill = event
    )) +
    geom_col() +
    geom_text(
        aes(label = if_else(n > 0, as.character(n), '')),
        position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5),
        color = 'white',
        size = 4
    ) +
    scale_fill_manual(
        values = c(
            'both' = event_colors[['Both']],
            'fireside_chat_only' = event_colors[['Fireside Chat']],
            'networking_only' = event_colors[['Networking Reception']]
        ),
        labels = c(
            'Both Events',
            'Fireside Chat Only',
            'Networking Reception Only'
        )
    ) +
    coord_flip() +
    labs(
        title = 'Event Selection by Employer',
        x = 'Employer',
        y = 'Registrants',
        fill = 'Event Selection'
    ) +
    theme_minimal()

employer |>
  distinct(industry, employer) |>
  arrange(industry, employer) |>
  group_split(industry) |>
  purrr::walk(function(df) {
    cat("\n\n### ", df$industry[1], " {.unnumbered}\n\n", sep = "")
    cat(paste0("- ", df$employer, collapse = "\n"))
    cat("\n\n")
  })

employer |>
  group_by(industry) |>
  summarise(
    employers = n_distinct(employer),
    registrants = sum(both + fireside_chat_only + networking_only),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    percentage = scales::percent(
      registrants / sum(registrants),
      accuracy = 0.1
    )
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(registrants)) |>
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c(
      "Industry",
      "Employers",
      "Registrants",
      "% of Registrants"
    ),
    caption = "Industry Representation Summary",
    booktabs = TRUE
  )

employer |>
  group_by(industry) |>
  summarise(
    registrants = sum(both + fireside_chat_only + networking_only),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(
    x = "Registrants",
    y = fct_reorder(industry, registrants),
    fill = registrants
  )) +
  geom_tile(
    width = 0.95,
    height = 0.95,
    color = "white"
  ) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = registrants),
    size = 4
  ) +
  scale_fill_gradient(
    low = "#FFF3E6",
    high = "#FF8200"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Registrants by Industry",
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    panel.grid = element_blank(),
    axis.text.x = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks.x = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "none"
  )

faculty |>
    select(first_name, last_name, job_title, events) |>
    mutate(
        name = paste(first_name, last_name)
    ) |>
    select(name, job_title, events) |>
    knitr::kable(
        col.names = c('Name', 'Position', 'Event Selection'),
        caption = 'Faculty & Staff Registrants'
    )

library(uuid)

render_id <- substr(gsub("-", "", UUIDgenerate()), 1, 8)

title: Private-Label Purchasing at Kroger
text:
Selected work / Team project



An analysis of household income and private-label spending, examining overall purchasing patterns and differences within Grocery categories.

Download R script

title: Private-Label Purchasing at Kroger
text:
Business Question
Do lower-income Kroger households allocate a larger share of their spending to private-label products than higher-income households, and is that difference concentrated in Grocery categories?

title: Private-Label Purchasing at Kroger
text:
Unit of Analysis
Our unit of analysis is the household.
We use households because income is measured at the household level. Each household therefore contributes one summarized private-label purchasing measure rather than households with more transactions receiving more weight.

title: Private-Label Purchasing at Kroger
Private-Label Purchasing at Kroger
text:
Basics
Read in tidyverse and data


View R code

library(tidyverse)

transactions <- read_csv("transaction_data.csv")
products <- read_csv("product.csv")
demographics <- read_csv("hh_demographic.csv")

Join data


View R code

data <- transactions |>
    left_join(products, by = 'PRODUCT_ID') |>
    left_join(demographics, by = 'household_key')

glimpse(data)

Initial EDA


View R code

## Count of private and national transactions
data |>
    count(BRAND)

## Count of transactions per department
data |>
    count(DEPARTMENT, sort = TRUE)

## Count of each income groups
data |>
    count(INCOME_DESC, sort = TRUE)

## Count of transactions with demographic info
data |>
    summarise(
        total_rows = n(),
        rows_with_income = sum(!is.na(INCOME_DESC)),
        percent_with_income = mean(!is.na(INCOME_DESC)) * 100
    )

Create new variable to track only private label product sales


View R code

data <- data |>
    mutate(
        private_sales = if_else(
            BRAND == 'Private',
            SALES_VALUE, 0
            )
    )

title: Private-Label Purchasing at Kroger
text:
Analysis
Rearrange data to household granularity


View R code

household_data <- data |>
    filter(!is.na(INCOME_DESC)) |>
    group_by(household_key, INCOME_DESC) |>
    summarise(
        total_sales = sum(SALES_VALUE, na.rm = TRUE),
        private_sales = sum(private_sales, na.rm = TRUE),
        .groups = 'drop'
    ) |>
        mutate(
            private_share = private_sales / total_sales
        )

glimpse(household_data)
summary(household_data$private_share)

Private label purchases by income groups


View R code

household_data |>
    group_by(INCOME_DESC) |>
    summarise(
        n = n(),
        mean_private_share = mean(private_share, na.rm = TRUE),
        median_private_share = median(private_share, na.rm = TRUE),
        sd_private_share = sd(private_share, na.rm = TRUE)
    ) |>
        arrange(desc(mean_private_share))

Distribution of private label dollar share


View R code

ggplot(household_data, aes(x = private_share)) +
    geom_histogram(bins = 30) +
    labs(
        title = 'Distribution of Household Private Label Dollar Share',
        x = 'Private Label Dollar Share',
        y = 'Number of Households'
    )

Private-label dollar share by income group


View R code

ggplot(household_data, aes(x = INCOME_DESC, y = private_share)) +
    geom_boxplot() +
    coord_flip() +
    labs(
        title = 'Private Label Dollar Share by Household Income',
        x = 'Income Group',
        y = 'Private Label Dollar Share '
    )

Income group summary


View R code

income_summary <- household_data |>
    group_by(INCOME_DESC) |>
    summarise(
        n = n(),
        mean_private_share = mean(private_share, na.rm = TRUE),
        median_private_share = median(private_share, na.rm = TRUE),
        sd_private_share = sd(private_share, na.rm = TRUE)
    ) |>
        arrange(desc(mean_private_share))

income_summary

Now you have an actual finding to work with — and it’s more interesting than a simple “lower income buys more private label” story.
Your descriptive results show:
Overall mean private label dollar share: 27.7% Median: 26.9% 100–124K is highest observed group at 30.2% Several lower income groups are around 28–29%
The highest-income groups are much lower:

150–174K: 22.7%
175–199K: 22.0%
250K+: 16.6%
200–249K: 16.3%

Last few groups have very small sample sizes, (especially 200–249K with only 5 households). Collapse in broader groups.
Establish broader groups


View R code

household_data <- household_data |>
    mutate(
        income_group = case_when(
            INCOME_DESC %in% c(
                "Under 15K",
                "15-24K",
                "25-34K",
                "35-49K"
            ) ~ "Below $50K",

            INCOME_DESC %in% c(
                "50-74K",
                "75-99K"
            ) ~ "$50K-$99K",

            INCOME_DESC %in% c(
                "100-124K",
                "125-149K",
                "150-174K",
                "175-199K",
                "200-249K",
                "250K+"
            ) ~ "$100K+"
        )
    )

Summarize new groups


View R code

income_group_summary <- household_data |>
    group_by(income_group) |>
    summarise(
        n = n(),
        mean_private_share = mean(private_share),
        median_private_share = median(private_share),
        sd_private_share = sd(private_share)
    )

income_group_summary

New plot


View R code

ggplot(
    household_data,
    aes(x = income_group, y = private_share)
) +
    geom_boxplot() +
    labs(
        title = "Private-Label Dollar Share by Household Income",
        x = "Household Income",
        y = "Private-Label Dollar Share"
    )

title: Private-Label Purchasing at Kroger
text:
ANOVA
Welch’s one way ANOVA best because of unequal sizes and different standard deviations


View R code

oneway.test(
    private_share ~ income_group,
    data = household_data,
    var.equal = FALSE
)

Welch ANOVA Result:

F = 5.7469
p = 0.003509

Average private-label dollar share is not the same across all three income groups.
Your grouped means are:

Below $50K: 28.9%
$50K–$99K: 27.2%
$100K+: 25.0%

So broad pattern is: Private-label dollar share decreases as household income rises.
ANOVA only tells shows at least one group differs, not which pairs differ.
Next step is a pairwise follow-up with Welch pairwise t-tests with a multiple-comparison adjustment


View R code

pairwise.t.test(
    household_data$private_share,
    household_data$income_group,
    p.adjust.method = "bonferroni",
    pool.sd = FALSE
)

Bonferroni-adjusted pairwise p-values:

$50K–$99K vs $100K+: p = 0.256
Below $50K vs $100K+: p = 0.004
Below $50K vs $50K–$99K: p = 0.173

Only statistically significant pair Below $50K vs $100K+
And the observed mean difference is 0.039 (0.289 - 0.250)
Households below $50K spend about 3.9 percentage points more of their total spending on private-label products than households earning $100K+. The middle-income group is not significantly different from either side after the Bonferroni adjustment.
Private-label dollar share differs across income groups overall, but the clearest difference is between households below $50K and households earning $100K or more.
Quantify key difference with confidence interval


View R code

t.test(
    private_share ~ income_group,
    data = household_data |>
        filter(income_group %in% c("Below $50K", "$100K+"))
)


$100K+ mean PL share: 25.05%
Below $50K mean PL share: 28.88%
Difference: about 3.83 percentage points
95% CI for $100K+ − Below $50K: -6.15 to -1.51 percentage points
p = 0.00133

Households earning below $50K spend about 3.8 percentage points more of their total dollars on private label products than households earning $100K or more. The 95% confidence interval suggests the true gap is roughly 1.5 to 6.2 percentage points.

Test whether those category gaps are statistically distinguishable.


View R code

commodity_tests <- commodity_data |>
    group_by(COMMODITY_DESC) |>
    group_modify(~ {
        test <- t.test(
            private_share ~ income_group,
            data = .x
        )

        tibble(
            difference = unname(
                test$estimate["mean in group Below $50K"] -
                test$estimate["mean in group $100K+"]
            ),
            conf_low = -test$conf.int[2],
            conf_high = -test$conf.int[1],
            p_value = test$p.value
        )
    }) |>
    ungroup() |>
    mutate(
        p_adjusted = p.adjust(p_value, method = "bonferroni")
    )

commodity_tests

Lower-income households allocate a larger share of Grocery spending to private label, with particularly pronounced differences in soft drinks, cheese, and fluid milk.

title: Private-Label Purchasing at Kroger
text:
Recommendation
Kroger should prioritize private-label positioning and promotion for lower-income households in high-volume Grocery categories where the income gap in private-label purchasing is strongest.
The clearest opportunities in this analysis are:

Cheese
Soft drinks
Fluid milk products

Kroger should also investigate why $100K+ households show lower private-label adoption in these categories.

title: Private-Label Purchasing at Kroger
text:
Limitations

Income is only available for a subset of households.
This is observational analysis, so income should not be interpreted as causing private-label purchasing.
Household composition, shopping frequency, store location, and assortment could also contribute to the observed differences.
The commodity analysis examines only five high-sales Grocery categories.

title: Private-Label Purchasing at Kroger
text:
Conclusion
Private-label dollar share differs across income groups. The clearest difference is between households below $50K and households earning $100K or more.
That gap becomes larger within Grocery and is most evident among the selected high-volume categories in cheese, soft drinks, and fluid milk products.
